claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloy films maintain structural and chemical stability at high temperatures through a synergy between short-range ordering and constrained grain-boundary mobility.
The proposed synergy suppresses grain coarsening.
The proposed synergy suppresses interfacial chemical segregation.
The test material consists of nanograined high-entropy alloy films with controlled grain-size distributions and defined grain-boundary character.
The films will be heated under inert or vacuum conditions to approximately 1200 K while being monitored by in situ TEM and synchrotron diffraction.
Approximately 1200 K is the alloy's solid-solution limit.
Grain-boundary structure, including interface nature and density, mediates high-temperature microstructural evolution.
Certain grain-boundary structures support short-range ordering.
Boundary characters that promote short-range ordering slow atomic diffusion across grain boundaries at high temperature.
Reduced grain-boundary atomic mobility limits grain growth.
Reduced grain-boundary atomic mobility prevents deleterious chemical segregation.
Boundaries conducive to short-range order will yield less grain coarsening than conventional boundary distributions.
Boundaries conducive to short-range order will yield less interfacial segregation than conventional boundary distributions.
The prediction is limited to inert or vacuum exposure up to approximately 1200 K.
Oxidizing environments may cause deviations from the predicted stability.
Phase transformations beyond the solid-solution range may cause deviations from the predicted stability.
The relative contributions of short-range ordering and reduced grain-boundary mobility to stability are not quantitatively determined.
A lack of differences between engineered and control films in grain growth, segregation, and short-range-order signatures would falsify the proposed synergy.
